title: Praying with the saints
hook: Catholics and Orthodox ask the saints to pray for them; Protestant churches pray to God alone

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary across the churches, and the Greek title Theotokos, God-bearer. Your line was all generations call her blessed. Whose yes did you notice? Day one thousand one hundred four.

Pray for me. People say it in hospital corridors, and text it before a job interview, and whisper it at a graveside. Paul says it in his letters, asking the Romans to strive together with him in their prayers. James tells his readers, plainly, to pray one for another. On that much, the text is clear. The question comes when the person you'd ask has died. Can you ask a saint in heaven to pray for you, the way you'd ask a friend down the hall? The churches answer differently. Today's word: intercession.

Intercession means praying on someone else's behalf, standing in for them before God. Paul urges it in his first letter to Timothy: "supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men." Here the road forks. Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask the saints to pray for them. Their reasoning: those who died in Christ are alive in God, not gone. So asking Mary or Saint Peter to pray for you is like asking a friend, a friend who is now very near to God. They are careful to say this is not worship; worship belongs to God alone. They point to Revelation, where elders before the Lamb hold "golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints." Protestant churches, following the Reformers, direct prayer to God alone. They point to the same letter to Timothy, a few lines later: "there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Protestants still ask one another to pray, gladly. They keep those requests among the living, and bring everything else straight to God through Christ. Then there's a verse both sides read closely, in Hebrews. After a long roll call of faithful people, Abraham and Sarah, Moses and Rahab, it says: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." Catholics and Orthodox hear the saints praying alongside the living. Protestants hear a crowd of examples, lives that still testify. Either way, the next words, "let us run with patience," put the runner in a full stadium, not an empty one.

Here's the practice: give thanks for a saint. Sit comfortably, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one person of faith whose life still speaks to you. It might be a saint from history, Francis, or Peter, or Mary herself. It might be a grandmother who prayed every morning, or a teacher who showed you what patience looks like. Recall one thing they did or said that you'd like to carry into your own week. Hold it for a while. If you pray, you can thank God for that life. If you don't, just say their name quietly, and keep the one thing. The bell holds the time.
Intercession. Praying on behalf of someone else. Every church here does it for the living; they differ on asking the saints to join in.
Your line: the cloud of witnesses. Today, ask one person to pray for you, or tell one person you're holding them in mind. Day one thousand one hundred four.

howItsDone: Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask saints, especially Mary, to pray for them, and keep saints' days through the year; Protestant Christians pray to God through Christ and ask fellow believers to pray for them.

Editor: 1 Timothy 2:1 is an exhortation, not Paul asking Timothy to pray for him, so 'asks Timothy for exactly that' became 'urges it'; Revelation 5:8 elders placed 'before the Lamb' as the verse says; the unexplained 'runner' now tied to Hebrews 12:1 'let us run with patience' (cited); practice reworded so it no longer repeats day 1098's 'remember them, give thanks by name' pattern.
Auditor: match prompt said "who said what" but the pairs are terms and verses; reworded. Quotations (1 Tim 2:1, 2:5; Rev 5:8; Heb 12:1; James 5:16) checked against the KJV.
